extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether claims set forth the subject matter the inventor (or joint inventor) regards as the invention and when to make rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112 (first and second paragraphs). Addresses evidence, omitted essential subject matter, and related rejections (written description, enablement, indefiniteness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that the claims define what the inventor regards as the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention set forth in the claims must be presumed, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, to be that which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rejection based on the failure of the claims to set forth the subject matter that the inventor regards as the invention is appropriate only where an inventor has stated, somewhere other than in the application as filed, that the invention is something different from what is defined by the claims. (See In re Moore, 439 F.2d 1232, 169 USPQ 236 (CCPA 1971); In re Zahn, 617 F.2d 261, 204 USPQ 988 (CCPA 1980).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence to the contrary — what can rebut the presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that a claim does not correspond in scope with that which an inventor regards as the invention may be found in statements outside the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of such evidence include contentions or admissions contained in briefs or remarks filed by applicant (e.g., Solomon v. Kimberly-Clark Corp., 216 F.3d 1372, 55 USPQ2d 1279 (Fed. Cir. 2000); In re Prater, 415 F.2d 1393, 162 USPQ 541 (CCPA 1969)), or affidavits filed under 37 CFR 1.132 (e.g., In re Cormany, 476 F.2d 998, 177 USPQ 450 (CCPA 1973)). The content of the specification is not used as evidence that the scope of the claims is inconsistent with the subject matter which an inventor regards as his or her invention. Agreement or lack thereof between the claims and the specification is properly considered only with respect to 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description/enablement) or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift in what inventor regards as the invention is permitted during pendency
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or the second paragraph of pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112) does not prohibit the inventor or a joint inventor from changing what the inventor regards as the invention during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims and submission of comparative evidence with respect to claimed subject matter which originally was only the preferred embodiment within broader claims have been permitted (In re Saunders, 444 F.2d 599, 170 USPQ 213 (CCPA 1971)). Continuation applications directed to originally disclosed subject matter that was not regarded as part of the invention when the parent was filed may still receive the parent's filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120 (In re Brower, 433 F.2d 813, 167 USPQ 684 (CCPA 1970)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unclaimed essential subject matter may trigger multiple types of rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim omits subject matter disclosed to be essential to the invention, different statutory rejections may be appropriate depending on the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omitted essential matter may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (first paragraph) as not enabling (see In re Mayhew, 527 F.2d 1229, 188 USPQ 356 (CCPA 1976)) or as lacking an adequate written description (see Gentry Gallery, Inc. v. Berkline Corp., 134 F.3d 1473, 45 USPQ2d 1498 (Fed. Cir. 1998)); under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (second paragraph) as indefinite (see In re Venezia, 530 F.2d 956, 189 USPQ 149 (CCPA 1976)); or under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as failing to claim the subject matter the inventor regards as the invention (see In re Collier, 397 F.2d 1003, 158 USPQ 266 (CCPA 1968)). Essential matter may include missing elements, steps, or necessary structural cooperative relationships described by the applicant as necessary to practice the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a claim omits matter necessary to practice the invention — follow written description/enablement guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim omits matter that appears necessary to describe the invention or to make and use the invention, examiners should consider rejections under the written description and enablement requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow MPEP §2163 et seq. (especially §2163, subsection I, and §2163.05) for written description issues and MPEP §2164 et seq. (especially §2164.08(c)) for enablement issues to determine whether a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (first paragraph) should be made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrelation of elements and indefiniteness analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that fails to interrelate essential elements of the invention as defined in the specification may be indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b), but lack of interdependence does not automatically render a claim indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Venezia, 530 F.2d 956 (CCPA 1976) for rejection where interrelation lacking. However, Ex parte Nolden, 149 USPQ 378, 380 (Bd. Pat. App. & Inter. 1965) and Ex parte Huber, 148 USPQ 447 (Bd. Pat. App. & Inter. 1965) show that a claim need not show interdependency, concurrency, or direct intercooperation among elements to satisfy 112(b). Use MPEP §2172 and related sections for guidance in determining whether an indefiniteness rejection is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to explain basis for rejecting as omitting inventor-regarded essential matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) for failing to claim the subject matter the inventor regards as the invention based on omission of essential matter must explain the basis for that conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must identify why the omitted matter is regarded by the inventor as essential and, where appropriate, identify where in the specification the unclaimed elements are described as essential. Failure to do so can lead to reversal (e.g., Ex parte Robertson, Appeal 2016-001938, op. at 4 (PTAB 2017)). Features labeled in the specification as preferred or illustrative are generally not critical or essential (In re Goffe, 542 F.2d 564, 191 USPQ 429 (CCPA 1976)). Broad disclosure language tends to rebut an assertion of criticality.
